steps.say: Microtia is grading from a small but complete ear to total absence. Grade one is mildly dysmorphic, grade two is partial with a narrowed canal, grade three is the classic peanut ear, and grade four is anotia with nothing present. The grade is deciding the reconstructive ladder.
steps.tx: **Microtia** (congenital underdevelopment of the external ear) is classified into **Grade I** mild dysmorphic pinna, **Grade II** partial development with stenotic canal, **Grade III** classic peanut ear, and **Grade IV anotia** (complete absence of the auricle). Grading sets expectations: higher grades need full framework reconstruction rather than minor reshaping.

steps.say: Cartilage reconstruction is waiting for the chest to grow. Surgery is timed from six to ten years of age, once the chest circumference is exceeding sixty centimetres. Earlier harvest is yielding too little cartilage, while the opposite ear is serving as a full-size template.
steps.tx: Timing of autologous costal cartilage ear reconstruction is held back until school age, from **6** to **10 years**, when a chest over **60 cm** guarantees enough cartilage to carve. Earlier harvest shortchanges the framework, while waiting lets the normal opposite ear reach near-adult size as a living template for height and detail.

rows: Enough rib to carve the frame

steps.say: The Brent sequence is building the ear in four sittings. Framework fabrication is coming first, then lobule transposition, then elevation with a skin graft behind the frame, and finally tragus and concha detailing. Four stages are spreading risk but are demanding patience.
steps.tx: **Brent technique** (the classic four-stage autologous rebuild) reconstructs the auricle in **four** stages: cartilage **framework** fabrication (carving and banking the ear shape), **lobule transposition** (moving the remnant into place), framework elevation with **skin graft** (lifting the ear off the head), and tragus and concha creation for finishing detail.

**Nagata technique** (the compressed two-stage autologous rebuild) completes ear reconstruction in **two** stages: **stage 1** fabricates the **framework** including the tragus with **lobule transposition** in one sitting, and **stage 2** elevates the construct with a **temporoparietal fascia** flap (the scalp blood layer) slipped under the skin. Two sittings suit families travelling far, but demand ample cartilage at once.
steps.say: Two sittings are completing the Nagata build. Stage one is fabricating the framework with tragus and is transposing the lobule together. Stage two is elevating the construct on a temporoparietal fascia flap. Fewer operations are suiting distant families.

The new ear is being carved from the child's own rib cartilage. The ipsilateral synchondrosis of the sixth, seventh, and eighth costal cartilages is supplying the block, with the slender eighth forming the helical rim. Tietze inflammation is shown here only to display the same costal cartilage anatomy.
steps.tx: Cartilage **framework** (the carved ear skeleton) is carved from ipsilateral **synchondrosis** (the fused cartilage bar) of the **6th**, **7th**, and **8th costal cartilages**, with the **8th** cartilage forming the **helical rim** (the curled outer edge). The sixth and seventh block builds the base; the eighth draws the rim. Careful harvest limits donor chest deformity.

vis.alt: Rib cage showing costal cartilages at the costochondral junctions used for ear framework carving.
vis.caption: Costal cartilages at the chest wall; the framework is carved from the 6th to 8th cartilages. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A plastic framework is avoiding rib harvest at a price. Porous polyethylene Medpor is offering a one stage alternative with no donor wound. But a lifelong risk of framework extrusion through thin cover is remaining, especially after knocks or infection.
steps.tx: Alloplastic **porous polyethylene** (**Medpor**, a plastic ear skeleton) framework provides a **one**-stage alternative avoiding donor cartilage harvest but carries a lifelong risk of **framework extrusion** (implant eroding through thin skin cover), worst after trauma or infection. Autologous cartilage integrates; plastic merely sits under cover.

**Prominent ear** deformity (**otoplasty** territory, not microtia surgery) corrects absent antihelical fold via **Mustarde** mattress cartilage sutures (folding stitches recreating the rim curve), and **conchal hypertrophy** (an oversized deep bowl) via **Furnas** concho-mastoid sutures (pinning stitches to the mastoid). Mustarde folds; Furnas pins back.
steps.say: A sticking-out ear is needing folding or pinning, not a new framework. Mustarde mattress sutures are recreating the missing antihelical fold. Furnas concho-mastoid sutures are pinning back a hypertrophic concha. Folding is correcting shape while pinning is correcting projection.

Numbers are guiding the rebuilt ear. Length is measuring five and a half to six and a half centimetres, tilt is running fifteen to twenty degrees off vertical, and projection is standing one and a half to two centimetres off the mastoid. The new ear is matched to these values and to its fellow.
steps.tx: Normal **auricle** dimensions (the target proportions for any rebuild) are **5.5** to **6.5 cm** in length, tilted posterior to the vertical axis by approximately **15** to **20** degrees, with **auricular projection** (stand-off from the head) of **1.5** to **2.0 cm** from the mastoid. The reconstruction is matched to these numbers and to the opposite ear.
